title: Cuban musicians, music and the theatre schedule
summary: Cubans admired American musicians; their music was big-band marches, calypso and rhumbas; he worked two shows a day confined to the theatre.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: They treated us very nice over there. But we just couldn't speak the language. I learned to speak about two or three numbers. I learned to speak about when I want rice -- "arroz." Or coffee -- "cafe con leche." Cold water -- "agua freer(?)." Different things, you know. Beefsteak was "bifsteak," and potatoes...

How about the interaction between your troupe, especially the musicians, and the musicians that were in Cuba, in Havana and in some of the other places? Did musicians come up and speak to you or speak to other members of the group?

Yes. All the places I've been, it's very... They treat the musicians very, very nice. And there's a lot... They're wild about the American musicians. But they figure American musicians are the top musicians... They have some top musicians in foreign countries who didn't have no name like they have here in New York, you know...
Mmm-hmm.
A lot of musicians here on New York, we... (what'cha call it)...we made history, especially the old-timers.
I see. Were they familiar with the kind of music that you were playing? Had they heard something llke it before? Did they have any recordings of people like
Moore (II) - 5
James Reese Europe, or even the Original Dixieland Jazz Band?

Yeah, they had quite a few. They were able to get over some of the records from the United States. And they did... As far as Dixieland or Swing music, they didn't know too much about that. Because they couldn't speak the language so good, some of them couldn't understand, you know...
What about their music? How did you find their music?
Their music is something like a big band style, big marches. And they had a lot of calypso stuff down there. A lot of rhumbas.
A lot of rhumbas?
They had a lot of rhumbas. Otherwise, it's Spanish... We called it Spanish music. That was Spanish music down there.
Did you feel that anything rubbed off on you from what the percussionists were doing with the large drums, the conga drums, and the small hand-drums?
Well, they had... They use a lot of bongos over there. And they used most of them, tall bongos, I guess about eight-nine-ten inches. You use them mostly with your hand.
Moore (II) - 6

Did you encounter any musicians over there who eventually went on to any fame? Like, I believe Arsenio Rodriguez... I don't know if that's too early for him. But he was a musician from Cuba who was very well-known; certainly in the Thirties he became known in this country. Did you know much about any particular musicians in the nightclubs?
No, I didn't know too much about them. Because we didn't get a chance to go around to nightclubs very much.
You were pretty much confined in your area.
Yeah. During that... We were confined in the theatre. They had two shows. They had a matinee, 3 until 8. Then we'd come right back with the night show, from 8:30 until 11.
That's a pretty full day.

Yeah. Well, during that time I was making pretty good money. I think the money during that time was very... I'm trying to remember what year. That must have been nineteen and...twenty...twenty-four...twenty-five... I can't remember the year now, it's been so long. It must have been around '22, '23, something in there.
